title: How Does Reasoning Flow? Tracing Attention-Induced Information Flow for Targeted RL in LLMs
claim: Aggregating attention into a answer-conditioned, flow-conserving graph reveals high-throughput tokens, which then guide token-level credit assignment.
layout: 2 regions, left-to-right then top-to-bottom; attention map zooms into flow graph
description: The left panel shows a lower-triangular grid of circular tokens, with rows labeled i and columns labeled j. Colored arcs link tokens, and the caption reads 'Aggregated Attention Map'. Token colors run from orange (question) through blue (reasoning) to yellow (answer). A pale blue wedge zooms from this grid into the right panel. The right panel shows a small flow graph with three labeled regions: Question (orange), Reasoning (blue) and Answer (yellow). Curved edges join the regions, and the label 'Attention-Induced Information Flow' sits beside the graph. Below it, a dashed box holds the equation sum flow_in = sum flow_out, with the label 'Answer-Targeted Flow-Conserving Normalization'. A grey arrow leads to a 'Throughput Ranking' podium icon. At the bottom, a response token row has dark arrows over the high-throughput tokens, above a gradient arrow labeled 'Response'. The label 'Credit Assignment on High-Throughput Tokens' marks the final step.
caption: Overview of FlowTracer. We build an attention-induced token graph, condition it on the answer to retain only routes that support the prediction, and normalize it to ensure locally consistent flow. Injecting flow from a super-source over the prompt to a super-sink over the answer yields a backbone of dominant multi-hop information paths. Token throughput on this backbone identifies key routing hubs for token-level credit assignment and reward shaping.
abstract: Token-level credit assignment remains a key obstacle for reinforcement learning (RL) in large language models (LLMs), where RL recipes typically treat all tokens equally, failing to distinguish decisive reasoning steps from routine formatting or fluent filler. Recent attempts leverage model-internal signals to assign finer-grained credit, but these are often point-wise heuristics that ignore the global structure of information propagation. We propose FlowTracer, an RL framework that traces answer-targeted reasoning flow on an attention-induced directed acyclic graph in which nodes correspond to tokens and edge capacities come from aggregated attention weights and derives token credit from this global structure. The edge capacities are reweighted to retain only the influence that can reach the answer region, while enforcing local flow conservation so intermediate tokens neither lose nor gain effective mass due to path length or irrelevant branches. On this graph, FlowTracer extracts an information-flow backbone connecting the question to the answer and scores tokens by flow throughput, revealing high-impact hubs and aggregation checkpoints that mediate long-range dependencies. These derived importances are used to shape token-level rewards, enabling learning signals to focus precisely on the tokens that route information toward (or away from) correct answers and delivering consistent performance gains across a range of reasoning tasks.
